title: No. 72 — The Same Subject Continued, and Re-Eligibility of the Executive Considered. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The administration of government, in its broadest sense, includes all the operations of the body politic — legislative, executive, or judicial. But in its more usual and perhaps more precise meaning, it is limited to executive details and falls particularly within the province of the executive department. The actual conduct of foreign negotiations; the preliminary plans of finance; the application and disbursement of public moneys in conformity with the legislature's general appropriations; the arrangement of the army and navy; the directions of war operations — these and similar matters constitute what seems most properly understood as the administration of government. The persons to whose immediate management these various matters are committed should therefore be considered the assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate. On this account, they ought to derive their offices from his appointment — at least from his nomination — and ought to be subject to his supervision. This view of the subject at once suggests the close connection between the duration of the executive magistrate in office and the stability of the system of administration. To reverse and undo what has been done by a predecessor is very often considered by a successor as the best proof he can give of his own ability and merit. Beyond this propensity, where the change has been the result of public choice, the successor is justified in supposing that the dismissal of his predecessor came from a dislike of his measures, and that the less he resembles him, the more he will recommend himself to the favor of his constituents. These considerations, together with the influence of personal confidences and attachments, would likely lead every new President to promote a change of personnel in subordinate positions. These causes together could not fail to produce a disgraceful and ruinous instability in the administration of the government.

With a positive duration of considerable length, I link the matter of re-eligibility. The first is necessary to give the officer himself the inclination and resolve to play his part well, and to give the community the time and leisure to observe the tendency of his measures and form an experimental judgment of their merits. The second is necessary to enable the people, when they see reason to approve of his conduct, to continue him in his post — to prolong the usefulness of his talents and virtues, and to secure for the government the advantage of permanence in a wise system of administration.

Nothing seems more plausible at first sight, nor more ill-founded on close inspection, than the scheme that, on this point, has had some respectable advocates — that of continuing the chief magistrate in office for a certain time and then excluding him from it, either for a limited period or forever after. This exclusion, whether temporary or perpetual, would have nearly the same effects, and these effects would for the most part be harmful rather than beneficial.

One ill effect of the exclusion would be a diminution of the inducements to good behavior. There are few men who would not feel much less zeal in the discharge of duty when they were conscious that the advantages of the office tied to it must be relinquished at a fixed point, than when they were allowed to entertain the hope of obtaining, by merit, the continuance of those advantages. This claim will not be disputed so long as it is admitted that desire of reward is one of the strongest incentives of human conduct, or that the best security for the fidelity of mankind is to make their interest coincide with their duty. Even the love of fame — the ruling passion of the noblest minds, which would prompt a man to plan and undertake extensive and arduous enterprises for the public benefit, requiring considerable time to mature and perfect — if he could flatter himself with the prospect of being allowed to finish what he had begun, would, on the contrary, deter him from the undertaking when he foresaw that he must quit the scene before he could complete the work, and must commit it, along with his own reputation, to hands that might be unequal or unfriendly to the task. The most that can be expected from most men in such a situation is the negative merit of doing no harm, instead of the positive merit of doing good.

Another ill effect of the exclusion would be the temptation to sordid views, to embezzlement, and in some cases to usurpation. An avaricious man who happened to fill the office, looking ahead to a time when he must in any case give up the income he enjoyed, would feel a temptation — not easily resisted by such a man — to make the best use of the opportunity while it lasted. He might not scruple to resort to the most corrupt expedients to make the harvest as abundant as it was brief. Yet the same man, with a different prospect, might content himself with the regular perquisites of his post, and might even be unwilling to risk the consequences of an abuse of his opportunities. His avarice might be a guard upon his avarice. Add to this that the same man might be vain or ambitious as well as avaricious. If he could expect to prolong his honors by good conduct, he might hesitate to sacrifice his appetite for honors to his appetite for gain. But with the prospect of inevitable removal before him, his avarice would be likely to win out over his caution, his vanity, or his ambition.

An ambitious man, too, when he found himself seated at the summit of his country's honors and looked ahead to the time when he must step down from that exalted height forever, and reflected that no exertion of merit could save him from this unwelcome reversal — such a man, in such a situation, would be far more violently tempted to seize a favorable moment to attempt the prolongation of his power, at every personal hazard, than if he had the probability of achieving the same end by doing his duty.

Would it promote the peace of the community, or the stability of the government, to have half a dozen men who had had credit enough to be raised to the seat of the supreme magistracy wandering among the people like discontented ghosts, sighing for a place they were destined never to hold again?

A third ill effect of the exclusion would be depriving the community of the experience gained by the chief magistrate in exercising his office. That experience is the parent of wisdom is an adage whose truth is recognized by the wisest as well as the simplest among mankind. What is more desirable or more essential than this quality in the governors of nations? Where more desirable or essential than in the first magistrate of a nation? Can it be wise to put this desirable and essential quality under the ban of the Constitution, and to declare that the moment it is acquired, its possessor must abandon the station in which it was acquired, and to which it is suited? Yet this is the precise meaning of all those regulations that prevent men from serving their country, by the choice of their fellow citizens, after they have, by a course of service, qualified themselves to do it with greater usefulness.

A fourth ill effect of the exclusion would be banishing men from posts in which, in certain emergencies of the state, their presence might be of the utmost importance to the public interest or safety. There is no nation that has not, at one time or another, experienced an absolute necessity for the services of particular men in particular situations — perhaps it would not be too strong to say, for the preservation of its political existence. How unwise, then, must be every such self-denying ordinance that prohibits a nation from using its own citizens in the way best suited to its needs and circumstances! Even without assuming the personal essentiality of the man, it is plain that changing the chief magistrate at the outbreak of war, or at any similar crisis, for another — even of equal merit — would always be harmful to the community. It would substitute inexperience for experience and would tend to unhinge and set adrift the already settled course of administration.

A fifth ill effect of the exclusion would be that it would operate as a constitutional ban on stability in administration. By forcing a change of men in the nation's highest office, it would force a change of measures. It is not generally to be expected that the men will change and the measures stay the same. The opposite is the usual course of things. And we need not fear that there will be too much stability while the option of change exists. Nor need we want to prohibit the people from continuing their trust where they think it can be safely placed — and where, by their constancy, they may avoid the fatal inconveniences of fluctuating councils and shifting policy.

These are some of the disadvantages that would flow from the principle of exclusion. They apply most forcefully to the scheme of perpetual exclusion. But when we consider that even a partial exclusion would always make the readmission of the person a remote and uncertain prospect, the observations made apply nearly as fully to one case as to the other.

What are the advantages claimed to counterbalance these disadvantages? They are said to be: first, greater independence in the magistrate; second, greater security to the people. Unless the exclusion is perpetual, there is no basis for inferring the first advantage. But even in that case, may he not have an aim beyond his present station for which he might sacrifice his independence? May he not have connections, friends, for whom he might sacrifice it? May he not be less willing, by firm conduct, to make personal enemies, when he is acting under the impression that a time is fast approaching when he not only MAY but MUST be exposed to their resentments, on an equal — perhaps inferior — footing? It is not an easy question whether his independence would be more promoted or impaired by such an arrangement.

As to the second supposed advantage, there is still greater reason to doubt it. If the exclusion were perpetual, a man of irregular ambition — the only kind of man we ever have reason to fear — would, with infinite reluctance, yield to the necessity of taking permanent leave of a post in which his passion for power and pre-eminence had acquired the force of habit. And if he had been fortunate or skillful enough to win the goodwill of the people, he might lead them to view as a very odious and unjustifiable restraint upon themselves a provision designed to bar them from giving fresh proof of their attachment to a favorite. We can imagine circumstances in which this discontent of the people, joining the thwarted ambition of such a favorite, could pose greater danger to liberty than could ever reasonably be feared from the possibility of his continuance in office, by the voluntary votes of the community exercising a constitutional privilege.

There is an excess of refinement in the idea of disabling the people from continuing in office men who, in their opinion, have earned approval and trust. The advantages of such a restriction are at best speculative and equivocal, and are outweighed by disadvantages far more certain and decisive.
